analysis.one_liner: Requires cars and light trucks to average 36 mpg by 2016 and sets rollover safety standards.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a vote: introduced in February 2002 with zero cosponsors, it sat in the Senate Commerce Committee until the 107th Congress ended in January 2003.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have directed the Transportation Department to raise fuel economy standards so that the combined average for new passenger cars and light trucks reached 36 miles per gallon by model year 2016. It would have closed two loopholes that let automakers count gasoline-and-alcohol 'dual fuel' vehicles and split their foreign-built fleets separately, created a voluntary registry for trading greenhouse gas credits, and required new federal safety standards for roof crush, seats, belts, and side-impact airbags, with the results shown on a consumer label. The bill was referred to the Senate Commerce Committee and never taken up.
analysis.who_benefits: Drivers, who would spend less on gasoline as new vehicles became dramatically more efficient; families, who would get safer vehicles with better roofs, seats, belts, and side-impact protection; and the public broadly, through reduced oil use and lower carbon emissions.

how_it_helps.text: Directs the Transportation Department to set annual fuel economy standards reaching a combined 36 mpg average for passenger cars and light trucks by model year 2016, with a default 36 mpg floor if the Department fails to write rules within two years.

Eliminates the 'two-fleet rule' that let automakers calculate separate fuel economy averages for domestically built and imported vehicles, and repeals the dual-fuel credit that gave makers fuel economy credit for alcohol-capable vehicles regardless of whether those fuels were actually used.

Requires NHTSA to write a rollover crashworthiness standard including dynamic roof crush limits, stronger seats and belts, side-impact head-protection airbags, and roof injury protection, and to put overall crashworthiness information on a window label buyers can compare.
Allows states to let solo occupants of hybrids or alternative-fuel vehicles use carpool (HOV) lanes.

analysis.who_pays: Automakers, who would face significant compliance costs to redesign their fleets to hit 36 mpg with the two loopholes closed; oil producers, who would see gasoline demand fall; and new-car buyers, some of whom would pay higher vehicle prices as makers recovered those costs.

drawbacks.text: Hitting a 36 mpg combined standard with the two-fleet and dual-fuel loopholes closed would require substantial redesign of the vehicle fleet, and automakers would likely pass part of the cost to new-car buyers.

The bill's greenhouse gas section is voluntary and market-based: it sets up a trading registry and lets companies bank emission reductions for credit against any future mandatory program, which critics of voluntary registries argue can soften future regulation rather than require cuts now.
Manufacturers could buy registry credits to offset up to 10 percent of the fuel economy standard for any model year, giving them flexibility that weakens the headline number somewhat.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The consumer case is strong: much lower fuel bills over the life of the vehicle, real safety improvements, and less oil consumption. The main costs fall on automakers and partly on new-vehicle prices, and the greenhouse gas trading title is soft — voluntary, credit-banking, and modest compared to the fuel economy mandate. On balance the bill's core provisions would have materially helped drivers and the public.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced on February 7, 2002, read twice, and referred to the Senate Commerce Committee, which never took it up; with zero cosponsors and no further action, it died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator John McCain of Arizona introduced the Fuel Economy and Security Act on February 7, 2002; it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation.
The Commerce Committee took no further action, and the bill received no committee markup, no floor vote, and no House consideration before the 107th Congress ended on January 3, 2003.
The fuel economy and safety provisions died with the bill, so the vehicle fleet standards and rollover crashworthiness requirements it contained were never enacted.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Automakers and oil producers kept the status quo: no higher fuel economy mandate, no closed loopholes, no new rollover safety requirements. Drivers continued paying for lower-mpg vehicles and got no new crashworthiness standard from this bill.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Automakers and oil producers kept the status quo

for.name: John McCain
for.role: U.S. Senator from Arizona and sole sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks; the bill was introduced on his behalf.

against.name: Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation
against.role: Committee to which the bill was referred
against.what_they_did: Never took the bill up: no markup, no vote, and it was never reported to the floor.

against.name: Automobile manufacturers
against.role: Industry facing the new fuel economy and safety mandates
against.what_they_did: Opposed raising fuel economy standards and fought proposals to raise CAFE during the 2002 Senate energy debate.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had a single Republican sponsor and zero cosponsors from either party, and it died in committee without any roll-call vote, so the record shows no partisan lineup for or against it.

industries.note: The bill would impose a 36 mpg combined standard by 2016 and close the two-fleet rule and dual-fuel credit the industry used to soften compliance, raising engineering costs — while drivers recaptured the cost through fuel savings. Its safety title would add roof-crush and side-impact requirements.

Higher fuel economy directly cuts gasoline demand, so the industry's interest ran against the bill's main purpose for consumers. The bill's stated aims included reducing reliance on petroleum used for vehicular fuel.

industries.industry: Carbon accounting, registries, and emissions trading firms
industries.note: The bill would create a national registry for greenhouse gas trading with certified registries, independent verification, and third-party auditors, creating a market for emissions measurement and trading services.
